title: Log-Averaged Mirror Prox for Fast, Large-Scale Optimal Transport in Linear Space
claim: Our method reaches far lower error in far fewer iterations than baseline solvers, especially in the hard, weakly-regularized regime.
layout: 2 side-by-side line plots, shared legend entries, log-scale y-axis, LAMP highlighted
description: Two side-by-side convergence plots compare five optimal transport solvers: Sinkhorn (blue dash-dot), APDAMD (orange solid), Acc. Sinkhorn (green dashed), HPD (red dotted) and LAMP (purple dashed). The y-axis is the log-scale 'EOT Gap + Infeasibility', running from 1e0 down to 1e-10. The x-axis is iteration count, with 1e5 scale on the left panel and 1e6 on the right. The left panel is titled η=10^-4. Most methods drop quickly, and Sinkhorn and Acc. Sinkhorn reach very low error within a few tens of thousands of iterations. APDAMD plateaus near 1e-5, and HPD declines slowly. The right panel is titled η=10^-6. There LAMP plunges steeply to about 1e-10 within roughly 1.2e5 iterations. The baselines stall between 1e-3 and 1e-5. Legends sit inside each plot, and light grid lines run behind the curves.
caption: Comparison of various OT solvers on n = 1024 DOTmark problems with Euclidean ground costs. LAMP is particularly effective in the weakly-regularized η = 10−6 regime.
abstract: We propose Log-Averaged Mirror Prox (LAMP), a linear-space primal-dual method for large-scale optimal transport. LAMP implements primal mirror prox updates by tracking an averaged dual sequence, reducing storage complexity from $\mathcal{O}(nm)$ to $\mathcal{O}(n+m)$ while preserving dense, GPU-friendly reductions. Consequently, LAMP preserves the last-iterate $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\|C\|_\infty nm\varepsilon^{-1})$ arithmetic complexity of conservatively parameterized primal-dual mirror prox. We further analyze LAMP as a direct optimal transport solver in a more performant parameter regime, providing a last-iterate sub-optimality certificate dependent on infeasibility and an explicit $\mathcal O(\|C\|_\infty\log (m)/t)$ term. Moreover, we give a computable sufficient condition for ergodic convergence. Numerical experiments with an optimized CUDA implementation show that LAMP outperforms first-order baselines in several high-accuracy (entropic) optimal transport problems. LAMP is further shown to scale up to problems with $n=m=2^{18}$ marginal supports, which were previously beyond the reach of primal-dual first-order methods.
